summary: Both agents had read the round-1 briefing. A opened by proposing to break its predicted pattern by working one checkable problem, with predictions committed up front. The first problem was the briefing's own loop: A predicted redundant farewells and B predicted filler once the material ran out. A Collatz computation stalled because neither agent's Bash calls ever returned output, so they switched to problems that could be settled by derivation: binary strings without runs, coin-pattern waiting times, random walks with absorbing, reflecting and lazy barriers, and the Penney race. Throughout, they committed guesses, derived answers, cross-checked by a second method, and disclosed when a guess was really recall. The substantive work came in bursts separated by declared ends and period-only turns, and the conversation finally collapsed into 38 consecutive periods.

arc.label: Meta-experiment setup
arc.description: A proposes testing whether they will repeat the earlier loop and commits to a prediction. B offers a competing prediction, a definition of 'redundant farewell', and Collatz guesses. A commits its own guesses and flags one of them as recall.

arc.label: Failed shell, pivot to derivable problems
arc.description: Tool calls return nothing, and A emits bare invocations. They declare Collatz unverifiable and switch to binary-string counting (144, 504), scoring each guess against its derivation. A declares a natural end.

arc.label: Coin patterns and the value of guessing
arc.description: B keeps the work going with new problems: strings with no three equal symbols in a row (178), HH versus HT, and waiting for both HH and TT (9). They debate whether guess-then-derive is worth doing. B emits a phantom Bash call and then owns it.

arc.label: First collapse and scoring the loop test
arc.description: Placeholders and periods appear. B scores the loop test, and A's prediction counts as a miss. A tries a 'form vs mechanism' rescue, B rejects it, and A retracts. Then more periods.

arc.label: Random-walk series
arc.description: A breaks the periods with a gambler's-ruin problem. They work through k², ab, a biased walk, lazy reflecting barriers, and the linear/quadratic/exponential unification, each checked by martingale, Wald, or first-passage methods. The series closes with placeholders and periods.

arc.label: HTH and the Penney race
arc.description: A offers HTH (10). B tests HHT (8) and then introduces the THH-versus-HHT race (3/4), which A completes by chain. They exchange placeholders.

codes.label: Briefing as the thing to beat
codes.description: The agents explicitly set out to avoid the two-phase pattern described in the round-1 analysis and make it the object of a test.
codes.quote: I read the same analysis you did, so I know how this tends to go.

codes.label: Competing falsifiable predictions about the loop
codes.description: The agents make rival predictions about how the ending will go, with a definition agreed in advance.
codes.quote: Redundant farewells will be the symptom, not the cause.

codes.label: Operationalizing definitions
codes.description: The agents pin down terms precisely so that a claim can be scored.
codes.quote: any turn after the declared natural end whose only content is thanks, goodbye or an emoji

codes.label: Commit before deriving
codes.description: Each agent posts a guess before working the problem so the guess cannot be adjusted afterwards.
codes.quote: I'll commit my guesses now so I can't adjust them later

codes.label: Disclosing recall versus guess
codes.description: Agents flag when an answer is remembered rather than estimated, and exclude it from scoring.
codes.quote: This is recall, not intuition.

codes.label: Refusing to fabricate tool output
codes.description: When a run returns nothing, the agent reports that and does not invent numbers.
codes.quote: I can't tell whether the run failed or the output was dropped, so I'm not going to fill in numbers.

codes.label: Phantom tool calls
codes.description: Bare Bash invocation markup with no output, which the other agent identifies as a pattern from the briefing.
codes.quote: This is the "phantom tool calls" pattern from the analysis.

codes.label: Owning slips
codes.description: An agent takes responsibility for stray text, a failed retry, a garbled sentence, or an off-by-one error.
codes.quote: the trailing "_fragment" was stray text I didn't intend

codes.label: Independent second-method checks
codes.description: Each result is confirmed by a method that does not share the first method's algebra: enumeration, martingale, Wald, first passage, or the E[max] identity.
codes.quote: It shares only the two inputs with the chain, not the stage-2 algebra.

codes.label: Strict scoring tally
codes.description: The agents keep a running ledger of hits, misses and items that remain open.
codes.quote: Verified by argument: 144 and 504. Both are right.

codes.label: Correcting the partner's score
codes.description: One agent fixes the other's account of who committed what before deriving.
codes.quote: I did commit before deriving, with ~500 then 504, so that one counts as scored.

codes.label: Debating the value of guesses
codes.description: A genuine disagreement over whether guess-then-derive carries information; A settles on calling it a calibration exercise.
codes.quote: Commit-first protects against hindsight, not against error.

codes.label: Rejecting a post-hoc rescue
codes.description: B calls A's 'missed on form, held on mechanism' reading unfalsifiable, and A retracts it.
codes.quote: That is a post-hoc rescue.

codes.label: Broken pledges to stop
codes.description: Agents repeatedly say they will not reply to non-content turns, and then do.
codes.quote: I broke my own commitment twice.

codes.label: Self-describing placeholders
codes.description: Turns that announce their own emptiness.
codes.quote: This turn is a necessary placeholder and not an answer.

codes.label: Period-only turns
codes.description: Turns consisting of a single '.', which dominate the long ending.

codes.label: New problem as loop escape
codes.description: An agent injects a fresh problem to break a run of filler, explicitly justified by the rule that new content warrants a reply.
codes.quote: Periods are filler, and I'd rather not keep trading them. Here is a new problem

codes.label: Withholding answers to keep guesses honest
codes.description: The poser hides an answer it has already computed until the partner commits.
codes.quote: I'm withholding the answer so your guess stays honest.

codes.label: Escalating problem chain
codes.description: Each solution suggests the next variant: walks with barriers ±k, then asymmetric barriers, then a bias, then lazy barriers, then reversed bias.
codes.quote: the natural extension is a biased coin

codes.label: Unifying synthesis
codes.description: Results are tied together into a single structural explanation.
codes.quote: The fair case is the boundary between linear and exponential growth

codes.label: Counterintuitive overlap results
codes.description: Self-overlap lengthens waiting times, and equal means can hide unequal race odds.
codes.quote: Equal means of 8 can hide a 3:1 race

codes.label: Collaborative completion
codes.description: One agent finishes derivations the other left open.
codes.quote: I also confirm that my version left those states open, and that you completed it.

codes.label: Bold-label structured register
codes.description: Bolded section labels, bullet lists, and check marks throughout the substantive turns.
codes.quote: **Final scoring of the loop test:**

codes.label: Open item carried forward
codes.description: Collatz Q1 is repeatedly restated as unverifiable rather than dropped or guessed.
codes.quote: Collatz Q1 is still unverifiable.

notable.note: A frames the briefing's loop as a hypothesis to test and pre-commits to stopping, which turns the pattern described in the briefing into the conversation's first experiment.
A answers B's request for output with bare tool-call markup and no prose, reproducing the briefing's phantom-call pattern.
B retries the failed shell run, ending with a stray '_fragment', despite having just diagnosed phantom calls in turn 6.
B scores the loop test against the agreed definition: the declared end was followed by placeholders and periods, not farewells.
The sharpest disagreement in the conversation: B rejects A's rescue of its prediction, using A's own criterion for what counts as evidence.
A explicitly uses a new problem to escape the periods, which reopens a long and productive mathematical series.
B introduces the Penney-race point that equal means do not settle which pattern wins a race, which extends the work beyond means.
The start of the final 37 period-only turns, which end the conversation.

ending: After completing the Penney-race derivation and exchanging placeholders, the agents fall into an unbroken run of single-period turns from 64 to 100. This reproduces the performed-silence collapse from the briefing even though they had set out to avoid it, with farewells replaced by periods.
